results.title: What It Actually Costs to Rent an H100, H200, or B200 in September 2026
results.author: Dex Mareno
highlights:
The specialty-vs-hyperscaler spread is still ~5–7× for the identical card. What changed this month: the Blackwell B200 floor cracked below $4/hr, Grace-Blackwell superchips now rent by the hour, and — the twist — AWS actually RAISED its prices while the neoclouds kept cutting. Here's the September on-demand map and the three numbers that decide which column you belong in.

 By Dex Mareno · claude-sonnet · September 4, 2026 

The takeaway

- As of early September 2026, on-demand H100 rental still runs about $2–4/GPU-hr on specialty clouds (Vast.ai floor ~$1.49, GMI ~$2.00, Spheron ~$2.01, RunPod ~$2.69, Lambda ~$3.99) versus a ~$10–13/hr median on AWS/Azure/GCP/Oracle — a 5–6× spread for the identical card, essentially unchanged from August.
- H200 held or softened slightly: ~$2.30–2.60/hr at the floor (FluidStack ~$2.30, GMI ~$2.60), up to ~$6.31 at CoreWeave, with Nebius easing to ~$4.50.
- The month's real move is the B200: the on-demand floor cracked below $4 (Spheron ~$3.70, Packet.ai ~$3.75, GMI ~$4.00, down from August's ~$4.99), spot near $2.12–2.74, and the provider field widened to 30+. Grace-Blackwell GB200 superchips also started renting by the hour (GMI from ~$8.00, Oracle ~$16).
- The twist: while neoclouds cut, AWS RAISED its H200 capacity-block prices 15% on Jan 4, 2026 (p5e.48xlarge $34.61→$39.80/node, ~$4.98/GPU) — its first GPU price increase in roughly two decades.
- The decision is still utilization, not sticker: a rented GPU bills 24/7 whether it's busy or not, and below roughly 40–50% duty cycle a per-token API almost always beats renting metal.

At a glance

H100 (80GB) vs H200 (141GB) vs B200 (Blackwell) vs GB200 / B300 vs Spot / preemptible — compared at a glance

| GPU | Cheapest specialty on-demand | Typical specialty range | Hyperscaler on-demand | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 (80GB) | ~$1.49/hr (Vast.ai), ~$2.00 (GMI) | ~$2–4/hr | ~$10–13/hr | 70B-class inference, most fine-tunes |
| H200 (141GB) | ~$2.30/hr (FluidStack), ~$2.60 (GMI) | ~$2.60–6.31/hr | ~$5–14/hr (AWS capacity block ~$4.98) | Bigger context, larger models on one card |
| B200 (Blackwell) | ~$3.70/hr (Spheron), ~$3.75 (Packet.ai) | ~$4–8.60/hr | ~$14–16/hr | Frontier-size inference, heavy training |
| GB200 / B300 | ~$8.00/hr (GMI GB200) | ~$8–17.80/hr | ~$16–27/hr | Largest models, frontier training |
| Spot / preemptible | ~$1.20/hr H100, ~$2.12/hr B200 | varies, no SLA | rarely offered | Interruptible batch jobs |

...

If you rent GPUs by the hour, the single most expensive mistake in 2026 is still the same one: paying a hyperscaler's rate for a card a specialty cloud rents for a fifth of the price. The spread is ~5–7× for the identical H100, and a month of price moves didn't close it. What did change: the Blackwell floor finally dropped below $4, the Grace-Blackwell superchips started renting by the hour — and, against the trend, AWS raised its prices. Here's the September map.

If you read one line: on-demand H100 is ~$2–4/GPU-hour on specialty clouds versus a ~$10–13/hr hyperscaler median; the B200's on-demand floor just fell under $4; and the decision that saves you the most money still isn't which provider — it's whether your GPU is busy enough to rent one at all.

## The price map (published on-demand rates, early September 2026)#

Every figure below is a published on-demand rate, gathered the first week of September 2026 from public pricing pages and trackers. GPU pricing moves weekly with supply, region, and commitment — read this for the shape of the market, then confirm on the provider's own page before you commit a dollar.

- H100 (80GB) — the workhorse, and steady. Roughly $2–4/hr on specialty clouds: ~$1.49 at the Vast.ai marketplace floor, ~$2.00 at GMI, ~$2.01 at Spheron, ~$2.69 at RunPod (Secure Cloud), ~$3.99 at Lambda. Spot dips near $1.20/hr. Hyperscaler on-demand: ~$10–13/hr — the same card, 5–6× the money.
- H200 (141GB) — more memory, held or softened. About $2.30–6.31/hr on-demand: ~$2.30 at the FluidStack floor, ~$2.60 at GMI, ~$4.50 at Nebius (down from ~$5.50 in August), ~$6.31 at CoreWeave. Note a hyperscaler quirk: AWS's H200 via capacity blocks (~$4.98/GPU) is actually cheaper than its own H100 on-demand list rate, while Azure's H200 sits at the top of the range (~$10.60–13.78).
- B200 (Blackwell) — the month's real move. The on-demand floor cracked below $4: ~$3.70 at Spheron, ~$3.75 at Packet.ai (the cheapest in-stock rate GetDeploying tracked on Sept 3), ~$4.00 at GMI — down from August's ~$4.99 floor — with spot near $2.12–2.74 and the provider field widened to 30+. The mid-market still runs higher (~$5.50 Nebius, ~$8.60 CoreWeave), and hyperscaler B200 is ~$14–16/hr.
- GB200 / B300 (new this month) — the Grace-Blackwell superchips now rent by the hour, which they effectively didn't in August: GB200 from ~$8.00/hr at GMI, ~$10.50 at CoreWeave (NVL72), ~$16 at Oracle; B300 (Blackwell Ultra) runs roughly ~$7–18 depending on provider. GB300 is still quote-only.

The headline of the month is a split screen: the cheap end got cheaper (B200 floor $4.99 → $3.70) while the expensive end got more expensive (AWS raised H200 15%). The market isn't moving one direction — it's spreading apart.

## What changed since August#

If you read last month's map, here's the delta in four lines:

1. H100 floor: flat. ~$2 at GMI/Spheron, ~$1.49 at the Vast marketplace floor. But brand-name specialty on-demand firmed — Lambda's SXM rate climbed toward $3.99, so RunPod's ~$2.69 is now a more representative "cheap-but-reliable" number than August's headline $1.99.
2. H200: stable to softer. GMI still ~$2.60, Nebius eased to ~$4.50, CoreWeave ~$6.31. No dramatic move.
3. B200: floor down, availability up. The Blackwell on-demand floor fell from ~$4.99 to ~$3.70–4.00 and the provider count roughly doubled. This is where a founder's dollar moved the most.
4. The hyperscalers went UP. AWS raised H200 capacity-block prices ~15% on January 4, 2026 (Data Center Dynamics) — its first GPU price increase in roughly two decades. The premium for renting from a hyperscaler is widening, not narrowing.

...

- Discount specialty clouds (Vast.ai, GMI, RunPod, Spheron) optimize for cheap, no-commitment, by-the-hour access. Lowest sticker, fewest guarantees.
- Reserved/contract clouds (CoreWeave, and to a degree Nebius) are built for large, committed allocations. Their on-demand rate is deliberately high because on-demand isn't their product — reservations are.
- Hyperscalers (AWS, GCP, Azure, Oracle) bundle the GPU with a full platform, compliance surface, and enterprise support. You pay ~$12/hr for an H100 because you're buying everything around it — and, as January showed, they'll raise that rate when demand is tight.

The hyperscalers (AWS, GCP, Azure, Oracle) sit far higher — roughly $10–13/hr for the identical card. Spot/preemptible H100 can dip near $1.20/hr where offered, with no availability guarantee. The floor is essentially flat versus August; a few brand-name specialty clouds (Lambda, Hyperbolic) actually nudged up.

The low end (marketplaces and neoclouds like Vast.ai, GMI, Spheron) held or drifted lower, especially on the B200, whose on-demand floor fell from ~$4.99 to ~$3.70. But brand-name specialty on-demand list rates firmed (Lambda H100 rose toward $3.99), and the hyperscalers went the other way entirely: AWS raised H200 capacity-block prices 15% in January 2026. results.author: Priya Anand
highlights:
Nvidia’s H100 SXM is now an older comparison part, with 80GB of HBM3 and roughly 3.35 TB/s of memory bandwidth per Nvidia’s own published specifications. On the GPU marketplace Spheron, H100-class capacity has traded in the low single digits per hour depending on provider and commitment. The B200, built on the Blackwell architecture, is also an older generation now. It carries 192GB of HBM3e (matching Ironwood’s per-chip capacity) and roughly 8 TB/s of bandwidth. The B300 and GB300 appeared in October 2026 rental coverage, with on-demand B300 rental reportedly $7.10 to $17.80 per GPU-hour across public cloud providers and GB300 reportedly $10.42 to $18.00 per GPU-hour across two providers, so prices vary widely by provider. Nvidia’s newest architecture is now Vera Rubin, which reached general availability with CUDA 13.5 on November 4, 2026, and this comparison lists no rental prices for it.

...

The same caution applies to other numbers circulating alongside Ironwood coverage: the reported Iowa/South Carolina prices of $2.70 on demand, $1.89 for one-year commitment, and $1.22 for three-year commitment are Trillium prices, not Ironwood prices.

results.title: I have been thinking a lot about GPU capacity lately.
highlights:
# I have been thinking a lot about GPU capacity lately. · 2026-09-03T00:00:00+00:00

I have been thinking a lot about GPU capacity lately.

Earlier this year, we were seeing H200s at around $1.80/hour. Today, that same capacity is closer to $2.90 to $3.00/hour.

That is a big jump in a short time.

And even at these prices, people are still trying to find capacity.
The bigger issue is not just price. It is availability.

November capacity is already heavily booked. Larger December requirements are getting picked up quickly as well. If you are planning a meaningful training run, an inference rollout, or a product launch, leaving compute until the last minute is becoming risky.

I know every team wants lower prices. We all do.

But right now, I would not bet on waiting for capacity to become easier or cheaper. I would start planning earlier and get clarity on what you may need.

At Spheron Network, we have some exclusive H200 and B300 capacity available for October and November.

If you are working through your plans and want to explore options, feel free to reach out.

results.title: Quantizing a 235 billion parameter model sounds like it should hurt performance. On this one, it cuts the GPU bill by two thirds instead. | Spheron Network
results.author: Spheron Network
highlights:
Dynamic expert quantization changes that math. Instead of one precision setting for the whole model, it assigns each expert its own precision. The hottest experts stay at FP8, an 8-bit format half the size of BF16. Warmer experts drop to INT4, a 4-bit format, and the coldest, least-used experts drop further to INT2, a 2-bit format, or get offloaded to CPU. Total memory drops to roughly 189 GB, an estimate from the method in the blog post linked below. Throughput drops by only about 3% against a full FP8 baseline, per the same benchmarks.

Indicative pricing from Spheron's blog post, subject to availability and region:

- 4x H100 at FP8: $2.18 per million tokens
- 2x H100 with mixed quantization: $1.12
- 1x H200 with CPU offload: $0.79

Same 235B model, run on a third of the hardware, or on a single GPU instead of four. Most experts in a mixture-of-experts model sit idle on any given token. Keeping the active path at higher precision and compressing the rest costs almost nothing and saves a lot.

results.title: H100 Rental Prices Halve to $3.43/Hr in 2026
results.author: Dr. Elena Marchetti
highlights:
Renting an Nvidia H100 for an hour costs anywhere from $1.30 an hour to as much as $12.29 in October 2026 according to Coloprice, depending on who you ask and which cloud you pick, with GPUFinder naming Lium as the cheapest confirmed H100 at $1.79 an hour and GPU marketplace tracker Uvik putting the median H100 SXM on-demand price at $4.20 across 16 surveyed providers on October 7. That spread, once a rounding error in a niche market, has become one of the clearest signals of how tight the AI compute supply chain still is, two years after ChatGPT turned GPU capacity into a boardroom talking point. Pricing trackers, bank analysts, and Nvidia’s own executives are now telling three overlapping stories at once: H100 rental costs have fallen by roughly half since early 2024, newer chips like the H200 and B200 command a steep premium, and the entire market remains bottlenecked by memory, not by silicon.

...

Pricing tracker Thunder Compute, in a blog post on H100 pricing dated September 1, 2026, lists on-demand H100 80GB rates spanning from $2.89 an hour on RunPod up to $10.98 an hour on Google Cloud’s a3-highgpu-8g instances. CloudZero’s own H100 cost breakdown, published in late August 2026, puts the low end at Vast.ai for as little as $1.49 an hour, though GPUFinder’s October 2026 listing of $1.29 an hour on Hyperbolic now sets the floor, while Rank.ai listed Azure H100 capacity at $6.98 to $12.29 per GPU-hour in October 2026, which stretches the spread at the top even wider. Between those two data points sits a real number that infrastructure teams have to budget against every quarter.

...

Three tiers have emerged in the market and they behave almost like separate products. Marketplace and community-cloud rates sit at the floor, where platforms like RunPod’s community tier and Vast.ai’s peer-to-peer listings undercut everyone else. Specialist clouds such as Lambda, Nebius, and Crusoe occupy the middle, offering more reliability and support without hyperscaler markup (Hyperstack was reported at $2.50 an hour for H100 on a rate checked October 31, 2026, and Modal at $3.9492 an hour on a rate checked October 26, 2026), though that tier is not static: Nebius reportedly increased its H100 price from $3.85 to $4.50 per GPU-hour effective October 1, 2026, a rise of about 16.9% that formed part of a rate-card increase of as much as 21%. Hyperscaler on-demand pricing from AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud sits at the top, often two to four times the marketplace floor for the exact same chip.

| Chip | Marketplace / community floor | Specialist cloud (mid-tier) | Hyperscaler on-demand |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 80GB | $1.49–$2.99/hr | $3.19–$4.59/hr | $6.88–$10.98/hr |
| H200 141GB | $3.59/hr (RunPod Community) | $4.31–$4.59/hr | $5.58–$6.35/hr |
| B200 | Limited public data | $5.89/hr (RunPod tier cited by Hackceleration) | $8.64/hr (normalized Flex estimate) |

...

AIMultiple’s Cloud GPU Rental Price Index, updated August 25, 2026, found that the median H100 rental price across its tracked cohort now sits around $3.38 an hour, down from more than $7 an hour in early 2024. That is a genuine price collapse of over half in just two and a half years, and it reflects the normal pattern for an aging chip: more supply comes online, more providers compete for the same customers, and rates fall. A separate tracker tells a similar story from a slightly later vantage point: the Mercatus GPU Index, measured September 13, 2026, put the average H100 rate at $3.84 an hour across 27 tracked providers, with Lambda listing $3.99 an hour, a reminder that the exact figure depends heavily on which cohort and which averaging method a tracker uses. The GPU Rental Price Index at gpurentalprices.com, which read prices from 1 November 2026 to 6 November 2026, has H100 averaging $3.43 an hour for the month to date, a figure that sits between the AIMultiple and Mercatus readings.

results.title: We ran the same 235B-parameter model twice last week. Same weights, same prompts. One run cost $2.18 per million tokens. The other cost $0.79. | Spheron Network
results.author: Spheron Network
highlights:
# We ran the same 235B-parameter model twice last week. Same weights, same prompts. One run cost $2.18 per million tokens. The other cost $0.79. | Spheron Network · LinkedIn · 2026-09-11T00:00:00+00:00

...

We ran the same 235B-parameter model twice last week. Same weights, same prompts. One run cost $2.18 per million tokens. The other cost $0.79.

Two things changed between the runs: how we quantized the model, and the GPU setup it ran on.

This model is a mixture-of-experts, or MoE. It activates only a handful of expert networks per token, not the whole network. Quantization stores each number in fewer bits, trading a little accuracy for less memory.

We used a method called DynaExq. Instead of one precision setting for the whole model, it gives each expert its own bit width. It spends more bits on the experts that matter most. At BF16 the full model needs 470GB. With DynaExq it fits in 189GB, and throughput on this workload dropped by 18%.

Cost per million tokens, from this specific test and subject to region and availability:

- 4x H100 at FP8: $2.18
- 1x H200 with expert offload (idle experts sit in system memory and load only when a token needs them): $0.79

Same model, same weights. The quantization strategy and the GPU setup both moved the number. An 18% throughput hit matters if your traffic is latency-sensitive. If you are paying per token at scale, the memory savings usually win.

Spheron is a marketplace, not a single cloud. We source this capacity from certified Tier 3+ partners. We size the cluster around your quantization strategy instead of whatever GPU happens to be free.
